sources.speaker: Alex Kantrowitz (Big Technology), quoting Dario Amodei, Michael Berry, Stephanie Palmer, Greg Diamos, Jack Clark, Jade Wang, Eric Schmidt and Jensen Huang
sources.locator: Full article opened via direct fetch and read end to end on 2026-10-04. Key passages: childhood and parents paragraphs; Caltech 2003 op-ed paragraph; father's death paragraph ('within four years'); Jade Wang paragraph; 'I get really angry' paragraph; Berry paragraphs ('most talented graduate student' is Kantrowitz's paraphrase; 'kind of a proud person' is a direct quote); OpenAI controversy paragraph (long documents, 'abrasive'); 'leaders of a company, they have to be trustworthy'; Huang exchange; Anthropic naming spreadsheet; SBF non-voting shares; Gulf states Slack quote; Claude 4 launch scene; closing 'The reason I'm warning about the risk' paragraph.
sources.excerpt: "Writing some website actually had no interest to me whatsoever," he tells me. "I was interested in discovering fundamental scientific truth." / "They gave me a sense of right and wrong and what was important in the world," he says, "imbuing a strong sense of responsibility." / "The problem isn't that everyone is just peachy with the idea of bombing Iraq; it's that most people are opposed in principle but refuse to give one millisecond of their time," Amodei wrote in The California Tech ... on March 3, 2003. "This needs to change, right now and without delay." / His father Riccardo, who'd long fought a rare illness, lost the battle in 2006 ... within four years, a new breakthrough turned the illness from something that was 50% fatal to 95% curable. / "It's the difference between his father most likely dying and most likely living, okay?," she says. / "I get really angry when someone's like, 'This guy's a doomer. He wants to slow things down,'" ... "You heard what I just said, my father died because of cures that could have happened a few years [earlier]. I understand the benefit of this technology." / But Amodei's penchant for poking at norms, and his strident sense of the way things should be, set him apart in an academic setting. Berry tells me that Amodei was the most talented graduate student he ever had, but his focus on technological progress and teamwork didn't play well in a system built to recognize individual achievement. / "I think internally, he was kind of a proud person," Berry tells me. "I imagine his whole academic career up until that point, whenever he did something, people would stand up and clap. And that was not really happening here." / A prolific writer, he'd produce long documents about values and technology, which some colleagues saw as inspirational but others saw as flag planting and heavy handed. ... Amodei, to some, was also too focused on maintaining secrecy around the technology's potential and collaborating with the government to address it. And he could be a bit abrasive, sometimes disparaging projects he didn't believe in. / "The leaders of a company, they have to be trustworthy people," he says. "They have to be people whose motivations are sincere ..." / "That's the most outrageous lie I've ever heard," ... "It's just an incredible and bad faith distortion." / Anthropic, a word that connotes being human centered and human oriented, is also there, and it also happened to be an available domain name in early 2021. / Amodei says SBF was an AI bull interested in safety, a good fit, but had sufficient red flags to keep him off the board and give him non-voting shares. / "Unfortunately," he wrote. "I think 'No bad person should ever benefit from our success' is a pretty difficult principle to run a business on." / Instead of a flashy presentation, he picks up a handheld mic, makes the announcement, reads his notes from a laptop, and then turns the spotlight over to Anthropic product head Mike Krieger. / "The reason I'm warning about the risk is so that we don't have to slow down," he says. / Working in Professor Michael Berry's retina lab, Amodei was so dissatisfied with the methods available to measure the retina's signals that he co-invented a new, better sensor to pick up more data. ... His dissertation won the Hertz Thesis Prize / "There was someone who worked on the cure to this disease, that managed to cure it, and save a bunch of people's lives," Amodei says, "but could have saved even more." / Amodei's father's passing has shaped his life's path to this day, says Jade Wang, who dated him in the early 2010s. / "The complexity of the underlying problems in biology felt like it was beyond human scale," Amodei tells me. / "AI, which I was just starting to see the discoveries in, felt to me like the only technology that could kind of bridge that gap," he says / "He believes that AI is so scary that only they should do it," Huang said. / (One such memo: an exploration of "M" companies vs. "P" companies, where Ms provide market-focused goods and Ps provide public-focused goods).
sources.context: A reported profile based on 'more than two dozen interviews with him, his friends, colleagues, and competitors', published the day before the companion Big Technology Podcast episode (S02). Quotes from Amodei are edited versions of the podcast speech (compare S02). The illness is called 'a rare illness' here; Amodei later named it hepatitis C (S11), which is not rare, so do not repeat 'rare'. Berry's 'most talented graduate student' line is Kantrowitz's paraphrase, not a direct quotation. The Gulf-states Slack quote originally appeared in Wired. The Jade Wang material is constrained by docs/content-analysis/entity-gaps/Dario-Amodei.md (protect, do_not_optimize): only her on-record quote and that she dated him in the early 2010s may be used. sources.title: If Anthropic Succeeds, a Nation of Benevolent AI Geniuses Could Be Born
sources.speaker: Steven Levy (Wired), quoting Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Chris Olah, Jared Kaplan, Demis Hassabis and others
sources.locator: Opened via direct fetch (WebFetch blocked) and read end to end. Page metadata datePublished 2025-03-28 (the draft and research notes say May 2025; correct the date). Key passages: family paragraph ('In the 1970s, their parents'); math obsession; 'anti-swayed' Rosewood dinner; GPT-2 'signpost'; 'One of the sources of my dismay'; 'he and six other OpenAI employees ... quit'; $124 million; held-back model 'It was costly to us'; Amazon/Google balance; OpenAI board merger approach; DVQ scene and two-day Machines of Loving Grace.
sources.excerpt: In the 1970s, their parents, Elena Engel and Riccardo Amodei, moved from Italy to San Francisco. Dario was born in 1983 and Daniela four years later. Riccardo, a leather craftsman from a tiny town near the island of Elba, took ill when the children were small and died when they were young adults. Their mother, a Jewish American born in Chicago, worked as a project manager for libraries. / "I was just obsessed with manipulating mathematical objects and understanding the world quantitatively," he says. / Daniela and Dario Amodei grew up in San Francisco's Mission District. (photo caption) / "I wasn't swayed," Amodei says. "I was anti-swayed. The goals weren't clear to me. It felt like it was more about celebrity tech investors and entrepreneurs than AI researchers." / "I didn't know if this model was dangerous," Amodei says, "but my general feeling was that we should do something to signpost that" / "One of the sources of my dismay," he says, "was that as these issues were getting more serious, the company started moving in the opposite direction." He took his concerns to Altman, who he says would listen carefully and agree. Then nothing would change, Amodei says. / Amodei realized he should have left sooner. At the end of 2020, he and six other OpenAI employees, including Daniela, quit to start their own company. ... Within a few weeks, a dozen more would bolt OpenAI for the new competitor. / most of the initial funding—$124 million— / "Our conclusion was, we don't want to be the one to drop the shoe and set off the race," he says. ... "It was costly to us," Amodei admits. / Amodei says that balancing Amazon with Google assures his company's independence. / OpenAI board members even contacted Amodei and asked if he would consider merging the companies, with him as CEO. Amodei shut down the discussion / So over the course of two frenzied days he banged out a nearly 14,000-word manifesto called "Machines of Loving Grace." / "We're not the prophets causing this to happen," he tells his team. / Even as a toddler, Amodei lived in a world of numbers. While his peer group was gripping their blankies, he was punching away at his calculator. / "Before, I was like, we're not building those systems, so what can we really do?" he says. "But now we're building the systems." / "My first thought," he says, "was, oh my God, could systems that are smarter than humans figure out how to destabilize the nuclear deterrent?" / "There is compelling evidence that the models can wreak havoc," he says. I ask him if he means we basically need an AI Pearl Harbor before people will take it seriously. "Basically, yeah," he replies. / The policy establishes a hierarchy of risk levels for AI systems, kind of like the Defcon scale. / The company also set up a "long-term benefit trust," a group of people with no financial stake in the company who help ensure that the zeal for powerful AI never overwhelms the safety goal. / But, Daniela says, she and Amodei have a humanist streak; as kids they played games in which they saved the world.
sources.context: Long-form magazine profile with on-record interviews and office visits. Independent of S01 in reporting, though both rely on Amodei's own account of the OpenAI exit. Wired does not name the father's illness or his town; 'Massa Marittima' (draft) is not supported here. 'Six other OpenAI employees ... a dozen more within a few weeks' contradicts the draft's 'fourteen researchers followed'. Describes the RSP as 'kind of like the Defcon scale' (not 'biosafety tiers'). Describes DVQ as a monthly session in October 2024 (biweekly by 2026 per S04).

sources.title: We Must Pace the Frontier
sources.speaker: Dario Amodei
sources.date: 2026-09 (page dated September 2026; published Saturday 2026-09-12 per S37 and S41)
sources.locator: Full essay opened and read end to end on 2026-10-04: opening paragraphs; 'over the last few months, I have become convinced'; three-step plan; 'Embedded Evaluators' section; 'Why Pace?'; 'Bottom Line'.
sources.excerpt: I feel the urgency personally. My own father died of a disease that was cured just a few years after his death, and I myself survived an early-stage cancer that would not have been treatable even fifty years ago. / Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. / But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence — not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up. We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain. / The idea of pausing or slowing AI has been floated as far back as 2023, and I think it made little sense back then. / The first step is something Anthropic is unilaterally committing to / But we are still the ones choosing what to include and omit. Embedded evaluators will change this dynamic. / Second Opinion. ... embedded evaluators can simply provide a second opinion free of commercial incentives. / we can't redact findings just because they are unfavorable. / Each frontier AI company commits to giving ongoing, employee-like access to a team of embedded third-party evaluators (such as METR) / Desks in our offices, access badges, and company laptops. / External reviewers should have the right to publish key findings about risk levels, incidents, practices, and the access they received or didn't receive — without editorial control by Anthropic. / My first concern is that, since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI. ... My second concern is the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident (OAI-HF) / To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress
sources.context: Policy essay published amid a week of public alarm (an Anthropic researcher's public resignation; the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident; S41). Discloses cancer without type, date or treatment; do not add any. Pacing is explicitly 'not halting'. Critics (S41) read it as market positioning.

claims.claim: Dario Amodei was born in San Francisco in 1983; Daniela was born four years later. Their parents, Elena Engel (a Jewish American born in Chicago who managed library renovation and construction projects in Berkeley and San Francisco) and Riccardo Amodei (a leather craftsman from 'a tiny town near the island of Elba'), moved from Italy to San Francisco in the 1970s. The siblings grew up in the Mission District.
claims.inference: Stable biographical frame for the opening sections. Use the birth year only; no full birth date is supported.
claims.alternative: The draft's 'from Massa Marittima, Tuscany' rests on Wikipedia (S44), whose cited Italian source (S47) did not contain it when opened. Use Wired's wording or verify the town before naming it. The FAQ's 'from Tuscany' is an inference from 'near Elba' and should be softened or sourced.

claims.claim: Wired reports that as a toddler he 'was punching away at his calculator', and Amodei says: 'I was just obsessed with manipulating mathematical objects and understanding the world quantitatively.'
claims.inference: An early, enduring preference for quantitative understanding. Consistent with a head-center type (5 or 6) and with the 5 reading's 'understanding first' motive, but it describes a cognitive style, not a motive.
claims.alternative: Talent and temperament of many scientists regardless of type; the toddler detail is the reporter's narration.

claims.claim: He says the dot-com boom around his high school years did not interest him: 'the idea of ... writing some website actually had no interest to me ... whatsoever. Or like founding a company.' He wanted to discover 'fundamental scientific truth.'
claims.inference: He did not set out to be a founder or executive; the CEO role arrived as a means. Supports reading his public role as instrumental rather than image-seeking (against Type 3).
claims.alternative: Retrospective self-narrative told in 2025, when a scientist-not-salesman image also serves him. The quotation differs between the podcast (S02, verbatim with fillers) and the profile (S01, edited); the draft must follow one source and cite it.

claims.claim: Amodei says his parents 'gave me a sense of ... right and wrong and what was important in the world', and that 'imbuing a strong sense of responsibility ... is maybe the thing that I remember most.'
claims.inference: Duty and responsibility are part of his own origin story. This supports a values-and-obligation frame that fits Types 1 and 6 more naturally than 5.
claims.alternative: Self-report about upbringing is not evidence of core motive; many people credit parents with values. The draft attributes the longer wording to the Big Technology profile, but only the podcast (S02 [41:51]) contains 'is maybe the thing that I remember most'.

claims.claim: He describes a very close childhood bond with Daniela: 'I think we decided very early that we wanted to work together in some capacity.' Daniela told Wired that as children they 'played games in which they saved the world.'
claims.inference: A lifelong trusted alliance precedes the company. Relevant to the Type 6 reading, where security is built through a small, reliable inner circle.
claims.alternative: A close sibling bond is common and does not discriminate type by itself.

claims.claim: Daniela Amodei told CNBC in January 2026: 'It's genuinely a privilege to run Anthropic with my sibling ... He had four years without me, poor guy,' and said Dario pushes her 'to think about the big picture' while she focuses on building an enduring organization.
claims.inference: Confirms the division of labor (he strategy and vision, she operations and people) from her side.
claims.alternative: The draft attributes this quote to the Big Technology profile; it is from CNBC (S43). Fix the attribution. Warm public framing by a co-founder during IPO preparation.

claims.claim: On March 3, 2003, as a Caltech undergraduate, he wrote in The California Tech that most students were 'opposed in principle but refuse to give one millisecond of their time' to oppose the Iraq war: 'This needs to change, right now and without delay.'
claims.inference: Early public moral urgency aimed at others' passivity. Fits a Type 1 reformer or a counterphobic 6; less typical of a detached 5.
claims.alternative: A single student op-ed during a period of campus activism; the original was not opened (quoted by Kantrowitz). Marre's later testimony (C15) cuts against a lifelong moral-crusade reading.

claims.claim: His father, Riccardo, 'was ill for a long time and eventually died in ... 2006', around the time Dario began his Princeton physics PhD (first months on cosmology). The death pushed him from theoretical physics toward biology 'to try and address ... human illnesses.'
claims.inference: The central consequential choice in the record: loss redirected his work toward preventing avoidable death.
claims.alternative: Career shifts also have intellectual causes; Wired (S03) says he had already concluded physics was 'too removed from the real world.' The death plausibly accelerated rather than solely caused the change.

claims.claim: On the cure-rate gap, Amodei said in 2025: 'Maybe three or four years after he died, the cure rate for the disease that he had went from ... 50% to roughly 95%.' Big Technology wrote 'within four years.' On August 15, 2026 he named the disease: 'I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him.' Sofosbuvir was approved in the U.S. in 2013.
claims.inference: The 'few years' of delay is the emotional engine of his urgency argument. The specific 'four-year' figure is his own estimate, so the H2 'The four-year gap' should be attributed ('by his estimate, three or four years') or softened.
claims.alternative: Sofosbuvir's 2013 approval is about seven years after 2006; earlier direct-acting antivirals (2011) raised cure rates in some patients. Do not 'correct' him in prose. Present the gap as his account. Big Technology's 'rare illness' wording conflicts with hepatitis C; avoid 'rare'.

claims.claim: Amodei: 'There was someone who worked on the cure to this disease, that managed to cure it, and save a bunch of people's lives, but could have saved even more.'
claims.inference: He frames delay itself as moral cost, which underlies 'warning so that we don't have to slow down' (C42).
claims.alternative: A rhetorically useful frame for an AI CEO arguing for speed; sincerity is supported by consistency across 2025-2026 sources but not proven.

claims.claim: Jade Wang, who dated him in the early 2010s, told Big Technology: 'It's the difference between his father most likely dying and most likely living, okay?'
claims.inference: Independent named testimony that the father's death shaped his path.
claims.alternative: Constrained by the entity-gap packet (protect, do_not_optimize): use only this on-record quote and the early-2010s dating fact; no relationship content, no speculation, no added FAQ emphasis. The draft's 'in the same profile' now follows an X citation and must name Big Technology explicitly.

claims.claim: Amodei becomes visibly angry when his motives are mischaracterized: 'I get really angry when someone's like, "This guy's a doomer. He wants to slow things down"' ... 'my father died because of cures that could have happened a few years [earlier]' (Big Technology, 2025). In the podcast he added that such critics 'completely lack any moral credibility' and 'it really makes me lose respect for them.'
claims.inference: Hot, moralized anger when his good faith is questioned. This is evidence against the detached Type 5 portrait in the draft and fits Type 6 (bad-faith and betrayal sensitivity) or Type 1 (anger at being judged wrong).
claims.alternative: Performative anger can be a communications choice in an interview about his public image. The profile edits 'a few years later' (podcast slip) to '[earlier]'; quote the bracketed profile version or the transcript, not a blend.

claims.claim: Amodei on his Stanford postdoc: 'The complexity of the underlying problems in biology felt like it was beyond human scale', and AI 'felt to me like the only technology that could kind of bridge that gap.'
claims.inference: Links the loss-driven biology turn to AI as a means of scaling scientific understanding.
claims.alternative: Retrospective rationale; many researchers moved to deep learning in 2014 for career and resource reasons (Baidu's $100 million lab).

claims.claim: At Princeton he co-invented a sensor to record retinal signals and won the Hertz Thesis Prize. Kantrowitz reports that adviser Michael Berry called him the most talented graduate student he ever had (a paraphrase, not a direct quote), and quotes Berry: 'I think internally, he was kind of a proud person ... whenever he did something, people would stand up and clap. And that was not really happening here.' Kantrowitz describes 'his strident sense of the way things should be' and a 'focus on technological progress and teamwork' that clashed with academic individualism. His doctorate was in physics/biophysics (thesis on the electrophysiology of neural circuits, 2011).
claims.inference: Pride and a felt lack of recognition in an individualist system, plus a preference for team science. The teamwork detail cuts against a lone-investigator Type 5 picture; the pride/recognition detail complicates any type.
claims.alternative: The draft puts 'the most talented graduate student he ever had' in quotation marks as Berry's words; it is Kantrowitz's paraphrase. The draft's 'Ph.D. in computational neuroscience' should read biophysics/physics. Berry's 'imagine' is speculation about Amodei's inner experience.

claims.claim: Princeton colleague Olivier Marre told AFP in October 2026: 'I never saw someone engaged in a strong moral or ethical quest' and 'Dario was ambitious, eager to succeed and be recognized for it, but not excessively or abnormally ... He wasn't a megalomaniac who crushed others.' Berry told AFP he was 'very idealistic...in a technical or scientific sense.'
claims.inference: Named contemporaneous-era testimony that weakens a Type 1 'moral crusader' reading of his youth and records a moderate recognition motive. Berry's 'idealistic in a technical sense' fits a head-center type.
claims.alternative: Retrospective testimony 15+ years later, given to a wire service profiling a now-famous CEO. Moral framing may have intensified with stakes and role rather than reflecting core motive either way.

claims.claim: Greg Diamos, who hired him at Baidu, says 'he really outworked everybody ... every waking hour and then some', had 'one of the strongest personalities of anybody in the group', 'didn't have a problem confronting much more experienced researchers', and that when he disagreed with the company's direction 'he would say it ... eventually the disagreement got to be so big that he felt like it was not worth continuing.'
claims.inference: A repeated pattern begins early: open disagreement with authority, then exit when trust in the direction fails (Baidu, Google, OpenAI). This counterphobic, confront-then-leave pattern fits Type 6 (or 8) more than the withdrawn 5.
claims.alternative: Baidu's lab also collapsed from turf battles (S01), so leaving had structural causes. Diamos is an admirer recalling a decade later.

claims.claim: Recalling the 2015 Rosewood dinner that led to OpenAI: 'I wasn't swayed. I was anti-swayed. The goals weren't clear to me. It felt like it was more about celebrity tech investors and entrepreneurs than AI researchers.' On AI risk at Google he changed his mind: 'Before, I was like, we're not building those systems, so what can we really do? ... But now we're building the systems.'
claims.inference: Skepticism toward charisma and celebrity authority, and willingness to update when conditions change. Both 5 and 6 are suspicious of hype; the 6 is specifically suspicious of leaders' motives.
claims.alternative: He later joined OpenAI anyway; retrospective self-presentation.

claims.claim: At OpenAI he was a prolific writer of long documents about values and technology, which some colleagues found inspirational and others 'flag planting and heavy handed'. Some thought him 'too focused on maintaining secrecy around the technology's potential and collaborating with the government to address it', and 'a bit abrasive, sometimes disparaging projects he didn't believe in.' Before leaving he wrote a memo dividing AI companies into 'Market' and 'public-good' types.
claims.inference: Writing as a way to organize others around his view, plus orientation toward government as the proper partner for managing risk. The government orientation fits Type 6's turn to authority structures under threat.
claims.alternative: Colleague criticism from an internal factional fight; 'secrecy' may reflect safety norms of the period rather than temperament.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that in 2016 Amodei argued that 'when it came to sensitive topics like how fast AI was developing, it would be better to tell the government first' rather than the public (Greg Brockman's account of the exchange).
claims.inference: If accurate, an early instinct to route danger through official authority rather than public broadcast. That is a Type 6 move, not a withdrawn Type 5 one.
claims.alternative: Reported from Brockman's side of a rivalry with unnamed sourcing; Amodei is not quoted. Amodei later became one of the loudest public voices, so the account may be selective.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that in 2017 Amodei was 'horrified' by staff cuts he 'considered needlessly cruel'; that he hired a policy adviser who proposed OpenAI as a coordinating entity toward 'an international coordination regime for advanced AI'; and that the idea of selling AGI to rival powers 'struck Dario as tantamount to treason, and he considered quitting.'
claims.inference: Loyalty and treason framing, plus an early impulse to build coordinating institutions. Prefigures the 2026 G7 request (C54) by nine years and undermines the draft's claim that the G7 was a turn away from his usual strategy.
claims.alternative: Anonymous-sourced; reported in a piece about the OpenAI feud. Use with attribution and without presenting private reactions as established fact.

claims.claim: Amodei told Wired that as safety issues grew more serious at OpenAI 'the company started moving in the opposite direction'; he took his concerns to Altman, 'who he says would listen carefully and agree. Then nothing would change.' He 'realized he should have left sooner.'
claims.inference: Trust broken by unkept agreement is his own stated reason for the exit. Betrayal-of-trust framing is a Type 6 marker.
claims.alternative: OpenAI declined to comment and maintains safety was constant. One side of a dispute.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that in 2018 'Dario agreed to stay so long as Altman promised that Brockman and Sutskever wouldn't be in charge', then learned of a conflicting promise; and that in late 2020 'Dario said he would accept nothing less than reporting directly to the board. He also said he couldn't work with Brockman.'
claims.inference: Conditional loyalty: staying in exchange for guarantees, then exiting when guarantees fail. Fits Type 6 (testing and securing commitments); the 'board only' demand could also read as 5/8 autonomy.
claims.alternative: Unnamed sourcing in a rivalry story; Amodei not quoted. Present as reported.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that at OpenAI Amodei 'didn't always feel properly recognized for his contributions', was annoyed that Brockman discussed the charter on a podcast 'despite having contributed less to it', 'got angry that he had been left out of the loop' of a 2018 meeting with Barack Obama, asked for a promotion to vice president of research with 'equal PR treatment' to the co-founders, and agreed in 2019 'not to denigrate projects he doesn't believe in that others want to bet on.'
claims.inference: Recognition and inclusion mattered to him. Marre (S14) independently describes him as 'eager to succeed and be recognized for it, but not excessively', and Berry describes a 'proud person' (S01). This complicates the detached Type 5 portrait. It is consistent with a 6's concern about being kept out of the loop, and with a modest 3 strand.
claims.alternative: Anonymous sourcing; credit disputes are normal in research labs and may say more about OpenAI's politics than his motives.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that after Altman accused the siblings of encouraging negative board feedback, then denied having said it, the exchange ended with 'the Amodeis ... shouting angrily at him.'
claims.inference: Hot anger at perceived dishonesty, consistent with C12 and C49. Not typical of a detached Type 5.
claims.alternative: Single anonymous-sourced account of a private confrontation; sensitive. Use, if at all, as 'the Journal reported' with no embellishment.

claims.claim: On leaving OpenAI, Amodei told Lex Fridman in November 2024: 'If you have a vision for how to do it, you should go off and you should do that vision. It is incredibly unproductive to try and argue with someone else's vision. You might think they're not doing it the right way. You might think they're dishonest. ... what you should do is you should take some people you trust and you should go off together and you should make your vision happen.'
claims.inference: The best single self-report on the 5-versus-6 hinge. Independence is pursued through a trusted group, not alone, and dishonesty is the named suspicion. A 5 can also 'go off' to build their own system, so the discriminating detail is 'take some people you trust'.
claims.alternative: General advice framed to avoid naming Altman; it also serves Anthropic's founding myth.

claims.claim: At the end of 2020 Amodei and six other OpenAI employees, including Daniela, quit; 'within a few weeks, a dozen more would bolt' (Wired). The WSJ says 'Dario, Daniela and nearly a dozen other employees' left; 60 Minutes says he left 'along with six other employees.' Anthropic has seven co-founders and launched with $124 million mostly from effective-altruism-affiliated investors. The name came from a brainstorm list; 'Anthropic, a word that connotes being human centered and human oriented' was chosen partly because the domain was available.
claims.inference: Corrects two draft facts: 'fourteen researchers followed' (and the FAQ's '14 colleagues' vs 'roughly a dozen') is not supported, and the name is not documented as coming from the anthropic principle.
claims.alternative: Headcounts vary by who is counted and when; use 'six colleagues, with about a dozen more within weeks' or 'a small group'. The anthropic-principle etymology appears in some secondary coverage but not in any opened source.

claims.claim: Anthropic has seven co-founders; Amodei gave them equal equity against advice and describes 'total and complete trust'. He divides the work: 'my job is the second [strategy, seeing what no one else sees] and Daniela's job is the first [operational execution]'. Daniela 'runs the company day to day'.
claims.inference: He secures his preferred work (strategy, thinking) by delegating human-contact operations to a fully trusted sibling. Fits both a 5's energy conservation and a 6's reliance on a trusted inner circle; the explicit emphasis on trust tilts toward 6.
claims.alternative: Standard founder division of labor; 'total and complete trust' was the interviewer's framing, which he endorsed.

claims.claim: In 2021 Anthropic held back a working model: 'we don't want to be the one to drop the shoe and set off the race ... We let someone else do that.' He admits 'It was costly to us,' calls it a 'one-off', and says that repeating it would mean 'We're just going to lose and stop existing as a company.'
claims.inference: A costly precautionary choice, then a pragmatic reversal under competitive threat. Shows the safety-versus-survival bind that recurs through 2026.
claims.alternative: Could be read as caution (6), conscience (1) or strategic reputation-building; the reversal shows commercial pressure dominating.

claims.claim: He repeatedly hedges against worst cases: he kept Sam Bankman-Fried off the board with non-voting shares because of 'sufficient red flags'; he says 'balancing Amazon with Google assures his company's independence'; and he declines to buy compute at his own optimistic forecast because 'there's no hedge on earth that could stop me from going bankrupt if I buy that much compute.'
claims.inference: A consistent worst-case-planning style in business decisions. Fits Type 6 (guarding against betrayal and catastrophe) and also Type 5 (conserving resources).
claims.alternative: Prudent capital management is expected of any CEO; the evidence is consistency, not uniqueness.

claims.claim: Bloomberg (via Quartz, October 2, 2026) reports Anthropic is considering super-voting shares that would give Amodei and fellow co-founders greater control after the IPO.
claims.inference: If adopted, it would secure founder control against public-market pressure, consistent with his pattern of guaranteeing independence through structure.
claims.alternative: Unconfirmed report of an option under consideration; common in tech IPOs.
claims.review_trigger: Check the public S-1 or final IPO terms when filed (expected around the Nov. 9, 2026 roadshow); drop or update the claim to the actual share structure.

claims.claim: On taking Gulf-state capital, Amodei wrote in an internal Slack message: 'Unfortunately ... I think "No bad person should ever benefit from our success" is a pretty difficult principle to run a business on.'
claims.inference: Reluctant pragmatic compromise. Cuts against a purist Type 1 reading; fits a 6 or 5 who accepts tradeoffs once the risk model favors it.
claims.alternative: A leaked internal message originally reported by Wired; tone may differ in context.

claims.claim: In November 2023 OpenAI's board approached Amodei about replacing Sam Altman as CEO and merging the companies; Wired reports 'Amodei shut down the discussion'.
claims.inference: Declining power when offered weakens Type 8 and Type 3 readings.
claims.alternative: He may have judged the offer unworkable or risky; Amodei has not commented.

claims.claim: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy uses 'if-then' trigger commitments, and Amodei says the RSP 'is checked by our long-term benefit trust'. He argues 'I don't think you can trust these companies to adhere to these voluntary plans on their own' and that 'the lack of uniformity is not fair to those of us who have put a lot of effort into being very thoughtful about these procedures.'
claims.inference: He builds pre-committed rules with an outside check on his own company and distrusts others' unenforced promises. Binding commitments plus external verification is a Type 6 signature; the fairness complaint has a Type 1 flavor.
claims.alternative: Commitment devices are also regulatory strategy (critics call it capture, S41). Wired compares the ASL tiers to 'the Defcon scale'; the draft's 'modeled on biosafety tiers' was not checked in an opened source.

claims.claim: Trust is a recurring organizing category in his own words across years: 'The leaders of a company, they have to be trustworthy people ... whose motivations are sincere' (2025); 'if you have a company of people who you trust ... you can really just be entirely unfiltered', versus a public world 'full of people who are interpreting things in bad faith' (February 2026); public distrust of AI is 'fundamentally a crisis of trust' and 'you have my word on that' (August 2026).
claims.inference: A decade-spanning preoccupation with sincerity, trustworthiness and bad faith, separating a trusted inside from a suspect outside. This is one of the strongest Type 6 markers in the record.
claims.alternative: Trust is also the explicit business problem of an AI company (enterprise sales, public opinion), so the vocabulary may be partly professional.

claims.claim: Jensen Huang said in 2025: 'He believes that AI is so scary that only they should do it.' Amodei replied: 'That's the most outrageous lie I've ever heard ... It's just an incredible and bad faith distortion.'
claims.inference: Same pattern as C12: reactive anger framed around lies and bad faith.
claims.alternative: Huang's critique (regulatory capture, control) is the main rival explanation of Amodei's policy activism and should stay visible alongside his reply.

claims.claim: His characteristic medium is long-form writing. He wrote the nearly 14,000-word 'Machines of Loving Grace' over 'two frenzied days'. 'The Adolescence of Technology', written over a winter break, is longer, about 20,000 words. Every two weeks he speaks to the whole company for an hour from a 'three or four-page document', and he writes extensively in an internal Slack channel.
claims.inference: Written-first thinking and communication. The draft's strongest Type 5 marker, but also typical of a head-center 6 with a 5 wing and of a scientist-CEO addressing 2,500 people.
claims.alternative: The draft calls Adolescence 'equally long' as Machines of Loving Grace; it is substantially longer. DVQ was monthly in 2024 (S03) and twice a month by late 2025-2026 (S38, S04).

claims.claim: Amodei says he spends 'a third, maybe 40%' of his time 'making sure the culture of Anthropic is good,' and that he speaks to the whole company every two weeks and answers questions.
claims.inference: Heavy, ongoing investment in group cohesion and shared belief. This sits poorly with a withdrawing, need-minimizing Type 5 and well with a 6's focus on a loyal, aligned group.
claims.alternative: A large company requires culture work from any founder-CEO; the share of time is his own estimate.

claims.claim: Bloomberg reported in June 2026 that Amodei 'has just one direct report' and that Anthropic is testing a leadership model 'where the CEO protects nearly all of his time for big-picture conversations, organizational culture, and giving input on research direction and strategy, rather than managing people in senior leadership roles.'
claims.inference: The most Type-5-consistent observation in the record: deliberate protection of time and minimal people management.
claims.alternative: Only the paywall-free portion was read. The arrangement also fits a 6 relying on one fully trusted deputy, and is a deliberate organizational experiment, not necessarily temperament. The identity of the direct report is not in the opened text.

claims.claim: He avoids personal publicity channels. At the May 2025 Claude 4 launch he 'picks up a handheld mic, makes the announcement, reads his notes from a laptop, and then turns the spotlight over' to a colleague. He wrote in August 2026 that 'I don't usually spend much time on social media', and AP noted he 'rarely posts on X' and did not respond when Greg Brockman challenged him there over the February 2026 Super Bowl ads.
claims.inference: Low image-management weakens Type 3. Reticence fits 5 and is also consistent with a 6 who distrusts the public arena as a bad-faith space (C34).
claims.alternative: Could be a deliberate brand strategy (the 'unvarnished' contrast with Altman noted by Axios, S42).

claims.claim: In 'Machines of Loving Grace' (October 2024) he wrote that he avoids grandiosity: 'I am often turned off by the way many AI risk public figures (not to mention AI company leaders) talk about the post-AGI world, as if it's their mission to single-handedly bring it about like a prophet', and that 'as a matter of principle it's bad for your soul to spend too much of your time "talking your book".'
claims.inference: Suspicion of single-actor power and of self-serving salesmanship, framed as principle. Fits 6 (distrust of unchecked individuals) and 1 (principle).
claims.alternative: Self-authored essay positioning; critics (Axios, S42) note the tension with his own vanguard role.

claims.claim: In July 2025 he called himself 'one of the most bullish about AI capabilities improving very fast' and said: 'Because we can have such a good world if we get everything right, I feel obligated to warn about the risks.'
claims.inference: Optimism and alarm come from the same model; warning is framed as obligation. 'Obligated' is duty language consistent with 6/1.
claims.alternative: The draft's contrast panel attributes 'We can have such a good world if we get everything right' to Machines of Loving Grace (2024). The phrase is not in that essay; it is from this 2025 podcast. Fix or remove.

claims.claim: In July 2025 he set a condition in advance: 'if we got a few years ahead in models and had only the alignment and steering techniques we had today, then I would definitely be advocating for us to slow down a lot. The reason I'm warning about the risk is so that we don't have to slow down.' In September 2026 he wrote that 'over the last few months, I have become convinced' that 'We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,' citing recursive self-improvement and the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. He told CBS: 'I don't think I fully just appreciated what it would actually be like when the progress was as fast as it was.'
claims.inference: A real change of position, made by his own pre-stated rule once observed conditions changed, with an admission that he underestimated the experience. It shows model-driven updating (head-center) under rising threat.
claims.alternative: Critics (S41) read the pacing call as competitive positioning; Axios notes Anthropic 'has gone back and forth' on unilateral slowing. Pacing is explicitly 'not halting'; the draft must not imply he wants to stop.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check after any industry pacing agreement, regulation, Anthropic model release or reversal of the pacing position; update the 'current position' wording.

claims.claim: The September 2026 essay commits Anthropic 'unilaterally' to embedded third-party evaluators with 'employee-like access' (desks, badges, laptops), the right to publish findings, and a 'Second Opinion' role. It explains: 'we are still the ones choosing what to include and omit. Embedded evaluators will change this dynamic', and 'we can't redact findings just because they are unfavorable.' He told CBS it is 'like a food inspector.'
claims.inference: He invites outside eyes into his own company and gives up control over what is disclosed. That runs against a Type 5's guarded boundary and matches a Type 6's search for external verification and a 'second opinion'.
claims.alternative: A pre-IPO credibility measure with commercial value; implementation details are not yet public. A Type 1 could also embrace accountability.
claims.review_trigger: Check whether embedded evaluators (e.g., METR) are actually in place and publishing; update if the commitment is implemented, narrowed or dropped.

claims.claim: He repeatedly says he is uncomfortable with private power, including his own: 'deeply uncomfortable with these decisions [about AI] being made by a few companies, by a few people' (November 2025). In September 2026: 'it has always been very strange that this technology is being built by a private company ... I agree with them. I'm uncomfortable', and he favors 'some kind of oversight, some kind of joint governance' by 'a combination of democratically-elected governments.' In August 2026 he wrote: 'At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power.'
claims.inference: Prefers impersonal institutions and shared oversight to personal or single-actor authority, including his own. A strong Type 6 marker (security through legitimate structures, distrust of concentrated personal power) and a poor fit for self-sufficient 5 or self-certain 1.
claims.alternative: Also a policy and PR position useful to a company seeking favorable regulation (Huang, Chamath and Emil Michael read it as control-seeking: S01, S41, S18).

claims.claim: In May 2025 he told Axios that AI could 'wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs — and spike unemployment to 10-20% in the next one to five years', adding: 'We, as the producers of this technology, have a duty and an obligation to be honest about what is coming.'
claims.inference: The warning is framed as duty. It is the forecast that made him a public figure.
claims.alternative: A forecast, not an outcome; present with its date.

claims.claim: At a May 5, 2026 briefing he offered a second mechanism (Jevons): 'If you automate 90% of the job, then everyone does the 10% of the job. And the 10% kind of expands to be 100% of what people do', while keeping the speed caveat: 'AI is moving faster than all these previous technologies ... it's possible you get these weird behaviors and this big disruption.'
claims.inference: He adds a model rather than retracting one, which suits careful head-center reasoning.
claims.alternative: Fortune explicitly offers the incentive alternative: 'the social and political cost of the bloodbath framing ... has made it more useful to suddenly sound a bit more optimistic.' Keep both readings.

claims.claim: Sam Altman told a Commonwealth Bank event in May 2026: 'we've been roughly right on technological predictions and pretty wrong on the social and economic implications', including on entry-level jobs: 'I'm delighted to be wrong about that.'
claims.inference: A useful contrast in how two CEOs revise forecasts.
claims.alternative: Comparison only; not evidence about Amodei's motive.

claims.claim: In February 2026 Anthropic aired Super Bowl commercials, made by the agency Mother, mocking chatbots that sell ads. Altman called them dishonest, and Brockman challenged Amodei directly on X; Amodei did not respond. Daniela Amodei presented the campaign on ABC's Good Morning America.
claims.inference: The institution, not Amodei personally, carried the public aggression; his silence fits his low social-media presence.
claims.alternative: AP describes 'a pair of TV commercials'; the draft's 'four-ad campaign' is unverified. No evidence on whether he approved the creative.

claims.claim: The WSJ reported in March 2026 that, in communication with colleagues, Amodei compared the Musk-Altman legal battle to 'the fight between Hitler and Stalin', called a $25 million Brockman donation to a pro-Trump super PAC 'evil', likened OpenAI and other rivals to tobacco companies knowingly hawking a harmful product, and wrote a Slack post calling OpenAI 'mendacious' and citing 'a pattern of behavior that I've seen often from Sam Altman.' Internally the brand strategy cast Anthropic as the 'healthy alternative.'
claims.inference: Private language is intensely moralized and organized around dishonesty and betrayal by a former ally. Consistent with C12, C24 and C34 and with a Type 6 (or 1) reading; inconsistent with emotional detachment.
claims.alternative: Reported from private messages via unnamed sources in a feud story; sensitive. Attribute to the Journal and avoid quoting the Hitler/Stalin comparison unless essential.

claims.claim: In the February 2026 Pentagon dispute he refused to drop two contract limits (no mass domestic surveillance, no fully autonomous weapons): 'we cannot in good conscience accede to their request.' He grounded the line in reliability and accountability ('frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons'; 'We don't want to sell something that we don't think is reliable'; 'we need to have a conversation about accountability, about who is holding the button and who can say no'), and in principle and patriotism ('We can't just be a total race to the bottom ... we have to have some principles'; 'It's about the principle of standing up for what's right'; 'Disagreeing with the government is the most American thing in the world. And we are patriots.').
claims.inference: Counterphobic confrontation with the most powerful authority available, justified through risk, reliability and accountability while affirming loyalty to the country. This blend of defiance and loyalty is characteristic of Type 6; the 'principle' language also supports Type 1.
claims.alternative: A business and legal position drafted with counsel; holding red lines can also be brand strategy. The draft's 'Dario insisted on' the restrictions in a July 2025 contract should be phrased as Anthropic's statement that the two uses 'have never been included in our contracts'.

claims.claim: On February 27, 2026 President Trump ordered agencies to stop using Anthropic technology, calling it 'a radical left, woke company'. Defense Secretary Hegseth designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk (formalized in early March), and OpenAI announced its own Pentagon deal within hours. Under Secretary of War Emil Michael called Amodei 'a liar' with a 'God complex' who wanted 'to personally control the U.S military'. Lawrence Lessig called the company's statement 'a beautiful act of integrity and principle'. Lockheed Martin said it would 'follow the President's and the Department of War's direction' and expected 'minimal impacts'.
claims.inference: Dated public consequences of the red-line choice; the hostile and admiring characterizations frame the strongest rival readings (control and arrogance versus integrity).
claims.alternative: Insults from a negotiating counterparty are not evidence of motive. Spell it 'God complex' as in the cited source. The draft attributes 'woke' to David Sacks; the opened source attributes it to Trump. Use Trump or open a Sacks primary source.

claims.claim: Anthropic sued on March 9, 2026 in the Northern District of California and in the D.C. Circuit. Judge Rita Lin granted a preliminary injunction on March 26 ('classic First Amendment retaliation') and on August 27, 2026 ruled one designation unlawful. On September 25, 2026 a 2-1 D.C. Circuit panel upheld the second designation. Anthropic said it is 'considering all options, including further review.'
claims.inference: Legal status current as of the accuracy check; the dispute remains split and unresolved.
claims.alternative: Court outcomes may change on rehearing, en banc review or Supreme Court petition.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check after any D.C. Circuit rehearing or en banc decision, Supreme Court petition, settlement, or rescission of either designation.

claims.claim: On June 12, 2026 an export-control directive arrived at 5:21 p.m. ET barring all foreign nationals, including Anthropic's own employees, from accessing Fable 5 and Mythos 5; Anthropic disabled both models for all customers. Its statement said the letter 'did not provide specific details of its national security concern' and that government should block unsafe deployments 'as part of a statutory process that is transparent, fair, clear, and grounded in technical facts.' Axios reports Commerce Secretary Lutnick called Amodei that day and Amodei called him back that night.
claims.inference: A sudden external loss of control over his work; the company response asks for fair, rule-bound process rather than exemption.
claims.alternative: The statement is the company's, not personally signed. The draft's 'Dario Amodei switched both models off for everyone' is a reasonable inference from his role but should not be presented as his personal act. The hook depends on a 2026 event; durability is better if the opening rests on a pattern.

claims.claim: On June 17, 2026, at a working lunch with G7 leaders in Évian-les-Bains, Amodei told them to 'resist the temptation to splinter' over advanced AI, according to the Financial Times citing unidentified people. He said he sympathized with efforts to keep AI from the wrong hands but that democratic nations should come together. Per the same summary, Altman emphasized providing cyber-defense tools to all countries present and Demis Hassabis called for US-led collaboration.
claims.inference: Under acute threat he moved toward a coalition of democratic governments and shared rules. This continues his 2017 coordination-regime instinct (C20), not a break from it.
claims.alternative: Closed meeting known only second-hand. The draft's 'Altman called for an international safety forum, and Demis Hassabis proposed a standards body' and 'coordinate trade in advanced models and share their benefits' are not supported by opened sources (the WaPo body is paywalled). Correct or remove them.

claims.claim: Axios reports that over a 20-day showdown Anthropic sent engineers to Washington, the federal Center for AI Standards and Innovation and the NSA required further fixes, and the models were released on July 1, 2026. A U.S. official said 'Anthropic eventually understood that in order to be successful, it needed to be on the same side as the government'; another source said 'There was never a moment when Dario stepped offstage', while policy chief Sarah Heck and co-founder Tom Brown took on more of the technical talks.
claims.inference: He stayed personally engaged with authority through the crisis instead of withdrawing; resolution came through institutional process.
claims.alternative: Government-side sourcing; the 'same side' line is an official's spin.

claims.claim: Anthropic said on June 1, 2026 that it had confidentially filed for a U.S. IPO. A leaked prospectus reviewed by Reuters showed a roughly $42 billion 2025 net loss on $4.6 billion revenue and referred to 'existential risks to humanity'; more than $34 billion of that loss reflected non-cash fair-value accounting adjustments. Bloomberg reported a pre-Thanksgiving listing target (investor day Oct. 14; roadshow week of Nov. 9; $1.8-2 trillion valuation), with dates 'subject to change'.
claims.inference: Places his warnings inside an investor document; context for Baker's critique (C57).
claims.alternative: Leaked and unofficial; IPO dates are fluid and Fortune mentions post-midterm timing. Do not present $42 billion as cash burn.
claims.review_trigger: Update when the public S-1 is filed, the IPO prices, or the listing is delayed; replace leaked figures with filed ones.

claims.claim: On August 15, 2026 investor Gavin Baker wrote that 'Dario has lost the argument' and, as the soon-to-be CEO of 'one of the most important public companies in the world', should be 'a more positive advocate for his own industry', while saying 'I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith.' Amodei replied the same day ('Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here'), rejected the claim that his messaging was 'disproportionately negative', named his father's hepatitis C, declined 'a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin', and conceded 'That is totally on us' about undelivered benefits, adding 'you have my word on that' and 'Honesty is the right thing on the merits.'
claims.inference: Under pre-IPO pressure he answered in public, courteously and at length, and spent a long-held private fact as a premise. The vocabulary (trust, word, honesty) matches C34.
claims.alternative: The disclosure also serves credibility with investors and the public. The draft links the first post for the illness disclosure, which is in the second post (S11); fix the link.

claims.claim: In September 2026 he disclosed: 'I myself survived an early-stage cancer that would not have been treatable even fifty years ago.'
claims.inference: A second private fact, again used as an argumentative premise ('I feel the urgency personally').
claims.alternative: Health information: do not add cancer type, date, treatment or speculation.

claims.claim: None of the reviewed interviews, essays, profiles or posts (2024-2026) contain a self-described diagnosis of autism, ADHD or other neurodivergence; the page should infer none.
claims.inference: Answers a reader search question without speculation.
claims.alternative: Absence in reviewed sources is not proof of absence; do not cite mannerisms as evidence of anything clinical.

claims.claim: In late September 2026 his public role became polarized and personal. Altman agreed the industry should 'pace the frontier' and Musk wrote 'Dario is right', while Chamath Palihapitiya said the essay was a case to 'concentrate enormous technological and economic power with Anthropic'. An SNL 'Weekend Update' sketch mocked him. Trump attacked him on Truth Social as 'pretending to be a "perfect little angel"' and later personally invited him to dinner. AFP notes some see 'a humanist' and others 'a skilled operator willing to exploit collective fears'.
claims.inference: Dated reception that frames the incentive alternative to a type explanation. Optional for the body; not personality evidence.
claims.alternative: Rapidly changing political context.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check before release and after the IPO or any White House meeting; remove items that no longer bear on the argument.

claims.claim: Asked about a friend's claim that he refused to watch Game of Thrones because it was not tied to 'impact', he corrected it: 'I wouldn't watch it because it was so negative ... I'm really excited about, like, creating positive sum situations.'
claims.inference: A small, specific preference: aversion to stories of betrayal and zero-sum cruelty. Mildly consistent with 6 or 1 and an anti-cynicism value.
claims.alternative: Minor anecdote; low evidentiary weight.

claims.claim: His characteristic first response to a powerful new capability is a threat scenario. On his scaling theory: 'My first thought ... was, oh my God, could systems that are smarter than humans figure out how to destabilize the nuclear deterrent?' On withholding GPT-2: 'I didn't know if this model was dangerous, but my general feeling was that we should do something to signpost that.' Asked by Wired whether 'we basically need an AI Pearl Harbor before people will take it seriously', he replied: 'Basically, yeah.'
claims.inference: Threat-first cognition that predates his CEO role and its incentives. This is the 6's scanning for danger, not only a job requirement.
claims.alternative: Safety research is his professional field; threat-modeling is a learned practice. This is why the discriminator rests on what he does with threat (C63), not on the presence of worry.

claims.claim: Interpretation (discriminator): across a decade, his repeated move under threat is to secure trusted allies and binding external structures, including structures that constrain him. Examples: urging government-first disclosure (2016); proposing an international coordination regime (2017); staying at OpenAI only against promises (2018); leaving with 'people you trust' (2020); RSP trigger commitments checked by a trust; equal-equity co-founders; asking the G7 for democratic coordination (2026); inviting embedded evaluators with publication rights; calling for 'joint governance'. He does not withdraw into private self-sufficiency.
claims.inference: This pattern discriminates Type 6 (security through trusted alliances, rules and legitimate authority, with counterphobic defiance when trust is broken) from Type 5 (security through withdrawal, minimized needs and private competence). It also overturns the draft's thesis that the G7 appearance was an unusual 'public turn'.
claims.alternative: Some examples are anonymous-sourced (S13); institution-building is also the job description of an AI-safety CEO and a regulatory strategy (critics in S01, S41). A 5w6 would show some of this; the weight of trust/betrayal language (C34) and hot anger (C12, C24, C49) is what tilts it to 6.

claims.claim: Interpretation: his anger in the record targets dishonesty, bad faith and broken promises (Altman's conflicting promise, 'mendacious', Huang's 'outrageous lie', the 'doomer' label, 'lack any moral credibility'). It does not target imperfection, sloppiness or rule-breaking as such.
claims.inference: Distinguishes a Type 6 reading (reactivity to betrayal and bad faith) from Type 1 (resentment at imperfection) and from Type 5 (cool detachment).
claims.alternative: The WSJ examples are anonymous-sourced; public anger can be strategic.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the real Type 5-like features are protecting nearly all his time, one direct report, written-first thinking, rare social media use, preferring strategy to operations and the childhood quantitative obsession. A head-center 6 with a strong 5 wing, a scientist's training and full delegation of people work to a trusted sibling explain them as well.
claims.inference: Keeps the strongest alternative honest: these behaviors are why Type 5 remains the main rival.
claims.alternative: If later sources show him withdrawing from engagement under threat, or describing energy depletion and boundary-guarding as his core concern, the 5 reading would strengthen.

claims.claim: Interpretation: both personal disclosures (hepatitis C in August 2026; early-stage cancer in September 2026) arrived as premises in public arguments about trust and urgency, after years in which long profiles left the illness unnamed.
claims.inference: Under Type 5 this reads as spending a reserved private fact when the argument needs it. Under Type 6 it reads as offering proof of sincerity to restore trust ('crisis of trust', 'you have my word'). Both readings fit, so it does not discriminate.
claims.alternative: Investor and IPO pressure gives an incentive explanation for the timing.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type 6. (1) The strongest Type 5 markers are well sourced. In 2026 he keeps one direct report and protects 'nearly all of his time' for big-picture thinking, culture and research direction rather than managing people (C38). His characteristic medium is solitary long-form writing: about 14,000 words in two days, a winter-break essay of about 20,000, biweekly talks read from a three-to-four-page document (C36). He rarely uses social media (C39). He prefers strategy, 'the thing that no one else sees', to operations (C27). He was a quantitatively obsessed child (C02). (2) He shows little of the visible self-doubt, reassurance-seeking or indecision often associated with 6. He is the 'purest believer' in scaling and holds 90% confidence against peers (S01, S04), and he acts decisively against the most powerful authority available (C50). (3) Much of the threat-modeling, institution-building and regulation advocacy is his profession and his company's strategy. Critics including Jensen Huang, Chamath Palihapitiya and Emil Michael read it as control-seeking or market positioning (C35, C60, C51). That incentive explanation competes with any type explanation. (4) Several Type 6 data points (C19, C20, C22, C23, C24, C49) come from one WSJ feud story built on unnamed sources. (5) Moral and duty language ('right and wrong', 'responsibility', 'cannot in good conscience', 'standing up for what's right', 'Honesty is the right thing on the merits'), the 2003 op-ed and Kantrowitz's 'strident sense of the way things should be' give Type 1 real support (C04, C07, C14, C50, C57). (6) Recognition concerns at OpenAI (C23) and Berry's 'proud person' (C14) hint at an image strand the 6 reading does not center.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 5 (the published reading) remains the strongest rival. It explains the lifelong drive to understand before acting ('fundamental scientific truth', C03; quantitative obsession, C02); thinking through writing and speaking from documents (C36); protecting his time and handing people management to one trusted deputy (C38, C27); low social-media presence and plain stage manner (C39); the preference for strategy over operations (C27); private reserve about personal life, including the father's illness left unnamed in long 2025 profiles, then disclosed only as argumentative premises (C66, C58); and skepticism of celebrity and hype (C17, C40). A 5w6 would add caution, threat-modeling and some loyalty to a small circle. Type 1 is a credible third: parental 'right and wrong' and 'strong sense of responsibility' (C04), the 2003 op-ed (C07), principled red lines (C50), fairness complaints (C33) and 'That is totally on us' (C57). It is weakened by Marre's 'I never saw someone engaged in a strong moral or ethical quest' (C15), the pragmatic Gulf-money compromise (C31), and his habit of grounding moral lines in reliability and accountability rather than in his own rightness (C50, C43).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does when security or control is threatened. A 5 reduces dependence: it withdraws, conserves, and relies on private competence and a guarded boundary. A 6 secures support: it tests trust, binds others and itself with rules and commitments, seeks legitimate authority and external verification, and confronts openly when trust breaks. Amodei's repeated move, from 2016 to 2026, is the second. He routed danger to government first and proposed a coordination regime (C19, C20). He stayed at OpenAI only against promises and left when they failed, taking 'people you trust' (C21, C22, C25). He built trigger commitments checked by an outside trust (C33). He asked G7 democracies to coordinate after the export shock (C54). He invited embedded evaluators who can publish what Anthropic would omit (C43). He calls for 'joint governance' over his own industry, saying 'I'm uncomfortable' that a private company holds this power (C44). The same axis shows in his emotional reactions. Hot, moralized anger recurs when he perceives dishonesty, bad faith or broken promises (C12, C24, C35, C49, C64), and trust and sincerity form a decade-long organizing category in his own words (C34). The time-protection and writing habits (C38, C36) are real, but a 6 with a 5 wing, scientific training and a fully trusted operator sibling explains them. A 5 does not easily explain the hot anger, the conditional-loyalty bargaining, or inviting outsiders past his own boundary.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: (1) Why someone so oriented to shared oversight also demanded to report only to the board at OpenAI (C22) and may seek super-voting control after the IPO (C30). Securing a safe base and grabbing control look alike from outside, and the record cannot fully separate them. (2) The recognition and credit sensitivity at OpenAI (C23) and Berry's 'proud person' (C14), which neither 5 nor 6 centers. (3) His steady confidence in his own technical forecasts against consensus (scaling; 90% on a 'country of geniuses'), which sits awkwardly with 6 doubt unless read as counterphobic certainty. (4) Marre's report that the young Amodei showed no visible moral quest (C15), set against the heavily moralized adult (C12, C49, C50). This suggests stakes and role amplified moral framing, which no type explanation fully captures. (5) How much of the safety-institution building is personality rather than strategy. The incentive explanation (C35, C60) cannot be ruled out from public evidence. Wing and instinctual subtype are not established: 6w5 is plausible but optional, and the draft's 5w6 and sp/so claims should be dropped or re-argued from evidence.
